But aside from the Bill altogether I would respectfully suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he should consider the desirability of empowering the board, as it was intended to empower it in section 20 of Bill (Q) so that it would have authority to take action in conditions of stress without reference to Ottawa.

My hon. friend from Moosejaw has cited as a parallel case the Board of Railway Commissioners, who may make rules and regulations. But those rules and regulations are subject to revision by the Governor in Council. The difference between the two is that before the rules and regulations can come into force in the one case they must be approved by the Governor in Council whereas in the other case they are subject to supervision and review by that body.
No difference.

Not in some respects because both are subject to the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council takes the responsibility for the action of the Railway Commission to that extent. But there is another point to be borne in mind. The Board of Railway Commissioners is largely a judicial body; and if the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) will consider that point, he will find that in all the legislation dealing with judicial bodies they are empowered to make rules and regulations, so far as they are not judicial which they are not always, but sometimes are subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. The great principle which underlies democratic legislation is that the executive, as well as the legislative bodies are subject to the will of the people. Therefore, I submit that in the administration of the Grain Act, which is so intimately related to the business of a large section of the community, the people should have some control over the board through the Governor in Council, and the board should not be free to do what it likes 'between sessions of parliament. It was suggested that the 'board should be independent of the Governor in Council. That suggestion is

hardly feasible in practical politics. Were these commissioners to be appointed from the party in opposition we might have an independent board to some extent; but until we shall have arrived at the millennium when those whom we appoint to office shall act without any consideration to the influences that may be exercised on them, we ought to follow the principle established by Democratic government and provide that these bodies which administer such important affairs must be held responsible to the government which has to account to the people.

I do not propose to go into the discussion as between the two Bills, but I have some interest in the progress of the idea of government by commission. commissioners greater confidence in themselves, and, while putting the responsibility on them would still hold them responsible to the government for everything they did. Under the present law there is an elaborate " and rigid system of furnishing the cars on the order principle, but there is ifo provision for doing the same in this case as is allowed in the case of grain which becomes heated in the elevator where relief can be given at once as the warehouse commissioner has authority to use his discretion to send cars sufficient to relieve the difficulty. I have strong representations asking that the same discretion be given to the warehouse commissioner under the existing special circumstances with regard to Mie grain I have mentioned. The representatives of the Grain Growers Association, who are here, were unanimously of the opinion that such discretionary power should be given as soon as possible, and if, on consideration, it seems to be the best thing to do, I shall ask the House to amend the Act so as to give that discretion at once to the warehouse commissioner. It seems to be a humanitarian way of dealing with the situation, and I don't see there can he any objection to it.
When will the amendment be brought down?

I will consider the matter, and if I find it necessary I shall probably submit it next Thursday.
Progress reported.

House in committee of supply.
Battleford public building, $10,000.
["If my hon. friend's statement were carried over the past four or five years, I think he would find that things are pretty fairly equalized.\nSome resolutions reported."]
Would the hon. minister give us information as to the progress of that building?

This is to cover the heating apparatus. The building is completed.
Battleford North public building, $10,000.

This is a revote to make provisions for the purchase of a site for a public building for post office and customs purposes. We intend going on with this building without delay as there is a very active demand for it.
Calgary-customs examining warehouse,

This is a very large item but the values of property have gone up very fast in the west. There seams to toe great demand for increased accommodation [for these offices, and sites are very expensive in Calgary and .all the western cities. This vote of $200,000 is towards .the purchase of a site and

the erection of a customs examining warehouse.

The present building in Calgary is occupied partly by the post office and partly for customs purposes. Is it the intention to use that building for customs purposes entirely and to erect a post office building somewhere else?
That is the intention.
Is there anything definite as to the location of the new post office?
No, nothing definite.

The item as it stands in the estimates, is rather misleading if the information given to me is correct. If a new site is to be bought for the post office and a new building erected, it will surely cost a good deal more than $75,000, while if the old building is to be .changed into a customs building, $200,000 will not be required for that. It looks to me as if the amounts have become displaced.
I do not think so. It is intended. to purchase a .site for the examining warehouse.
As far as I can judge, it will cost $100,000 to get the site for a post office. If the vote of $75,000 is intended to meet the requirements of the post office, it will be absolutely inadequate.
As far as I can judge, it would cost $100,000 to get the site, and you would be left with an inadequate sum for the erection of the post office.
This, I think, merely provides for the purchase of the site of the examining warehouse and to start the building.

In the former estimates there was an item for the erection of an immigration building in Calgary which is apparently left out of these estimates. The immigration building at present used in Calgary is entirely inadequate and is not creditable to the Dominion government. There is a very urgent need for a new building, and I would strongly urge the minister to make even a larger appropriation than was in the former estimates for that purpose.

I will make a note of my hon. friend's statement.
Calgary-new post office, $75,000.
This is a revote, nothing having been spent of the vote of last year.

If $200,000 is required to purchase a site for an examining warehouse and to start the building, certainly
more than $75,000 is required for a post office site, whi-ch must necessarily be in a more central position. It seems to me the respective amounts are out of proportion.
It may be there is some mistake; if so, we will try to correct it. _ I fancy that the reason is that the old site of the post office may be used for the erec tion of a new one.

There is a building on
ithe site now-a tour story building, I think; certainly not less than three stories.
It is absolutely inadequate for the service.
Is it intended to tear it down and use the site again?
Either tear it down or remodel it completely.

The only thing I desire is that the minister deal with the matter promptly and liberally because the necessities of the case are very urgent.
Edmonton-new drill hall, $50,000.
In what position does this matter stand? I understand the city has made the offer of a site, and I am rather anxious to know that this money, voted and re-voted, is to be expended.

It is intended to expend this sum without delay. The city of Edmonton as my hon. friend knows, purchased the site on the Hudson's Bay Company's reserve. We have a considerable number of regiments in Edmonton. I can only say that it is intended to use this money. The city having purchased the site, it would foe, no doubt, a part of our contract to proceed with the erection of the building without delay.

I desire to bring before the minister the question of the Moosejaw armoury and drill hall. For three or four years past an item has been in the estimates for the commencement of an armoury in that city. The reason that the work was not proceeded with is that the city was to donate the site and there were conveyancing difficulties in the way of securing the place. Last year, the site was secured and the way was opened for the work of construction. Much to my surprise, in these estimates, the first since it was possible to make the vote efficacious, I find that the item is dropped. As I have said, it appeared for three or four years, beginning at $15,000 and going up to $30,000 as the needs of the city grew greater. I have here the Moosejaw ' Morning News ' of January 23, 1912. This is a paper which supports the present government. A deputation was sent from the Board of Trade of Moosejaw to interview the government. I do not know that they interview-

ed the Minister of Public Works, but they certainly saw the Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes). The following is from the account of the interview with the chief spokesman of the delegation of four who came to Ottawa:-

Willoughby, who went to Ottawa as a member of the Board of Trade deputation, returned to the city yesterday afternoon. Interviewed by the ' News,' he declined to make a general statement of the result of his visit, as it is his intention to report to-the Board of Trade.
He intimated, however, that as a result of the deputation's interview with the Minister of Militia, Moose jaw was promised a $75,000 armoury and drill shed.
Is it the intention,, therefore, to provide in the supplementary estimates for such an armoury and drill .stood as is alleged in this paper to have been promised?

I did not have the advantage of meeting that deputation. Of course, if the site has been furnished to us after negotiation by the civic authorities, I should imagine the government's duty would be to erect the armoury as soon as possible. There wild be supplementary estimates; and I am anxious to satisfy, as far as possible, the Claims of the country. But I am not the sole arbiter of either the [DOT]main or the supplementary estimates. I tell the hon, gentleman only what he, no doubt, already knows when I say that there are very great demands this year for the equipment o,f harbours and other matters in connection with transportation; and although it is necessary to put our militia on a proper footing and provide armouries as .far as possible, it might be argued that the necessities to which I have referred *are more pressing. I will make a note of what the hon. gentleman says. I am not in a position to say what the supplementary .estimates will contain.
Could not the minister give some reason why the item is dropped after hawing been recognized by the government and the House for so many years?

It is done under the pressure of the urgent needs of which I have spoken. The opening of the Panama canal, it is supposed, will create a demand for much additional shipping on the Pacific, and we have been urged very strongly to improve our western ports which are now inadequate. On toe great lakes the demand is the same, and so it is for the ports on the Atlantic. That is the only reason I can think of.

Will the hon. minister consult with the Minister of Militia .and Defence with regard to this alleged promise, and inform me, on some later occasion, whether such a promise was made, and if it will be duly implemented?

In the estimates for 191112, there was an item of $17,500 for the Sarnia armoury. That is omitted from the estimates before the House. The .minister (Mr. Monk) say.s that a good many of these items for armouries have been left out because of the needs .for expenditures on the aids to navigation. I .may point out that the appropriation for Sarnia harbour has also been cut out of these estimates. I should be glad, at the proper time, to hear an explanation of this.
As to the armoury .and the harbour improvement, that is under .consideration, and I hope provision will be made iin the supplementary estimates.

In connection with the armoury at Moosejaw, I would ask the government what its policy is with reference to acquiring free sites for armoury and drill hall purposes.
I understand from the discussion that has taken place that the city of Moosejaw is making a free grant to the government for such a purpose. I would like to know whether it is the policy of the government to erect drill halls in all places which give free grants to the government, and if that is the policy, is it also the policy of^ the government to decline to erect drill halls in other places until free grants are made to the government?

The policy of the government on that point has not come up for consideration or discussion; the government has not yet had occasion to go fully into the matter and adopt a policy upon that point. But I may inform my hon. friend that my own opinion, so far as I have been able to form an opinion upon the subject, is that we should- be prepared to supply armouries where the city goes to the trouble and expense of providing the grant of a site. I would even go further, and say that where public buildings are wanted, and the city is in a position to offer us the grant of a site, we should be prepared to respond by providing the building, where conditions suitable for the erection of such a building exist. We are continually having a great deal of difficulty in those matters, very often prices are put up for the site. I favour the idea that where the municipality offers a site for a public building or an armoury, we ought to be prepared to meet the city authorities half way.

I agree with my hon. friend that it is desirable if cities or towns can make free grants of sites that those grants should be accepted by the government, and that the government should do what it can towards the erection of drill halls or armouries. There are some cities which are better circum-

stanced than others in possessing lands *which can be used as sites for armouries and drill halls; and the case of the city of Moosejaw is one in point. Last session I asked a question in the House, at page 3,281 of ' Hansard,' whether any free grant had been made by the Dominion government to the city of Moosejaw; and the answer which I received from the then Minister of the Interior was that 2,152 lots had peen patented to the city of Moosejaw as a free grant by the Dominion government, under an order in council dated 6th April, 1903. What I want to point out is that such a city as Moosejaw, which received a grant from the Dominion government of 2,152 town lots, is in a position to make a free grant for such a purpose, and may well toe expected to do so. I might also mention the city of Regina, although it is not before us in this item. I understand that Regina has also made a free grant to the Dominion government for such a purpose. In the same question which I asked last session, I got an answer from the Minister of the Interior that the Dominion government had patented to the city of Regina 4,863 town lots; and in addition to these lots, 285.55 acres of the unsubdivided portion of the townsite of Regina were revested in the Crown and subsequently patented to the city of Regina. I want to point out to the minister that if the city of Moosejaw and the city of Regina are in a position to make free grants to the government, and may be properly expected to do so, there are other cities in the Northwest which have not received grants from this government, and which cannot be expected to make free grants for such purposes. I appreciate what the minister has said that there is danger of the government being held up. But I am sure that the municipal authorities in each case may be relied upon to assist the government in the purchase of sites. In my own city of Saskatoon a site was purchased, composing about an acre of land, and having on it one of the best houses in the city, which could be used for temporary purposes. The price paid by this government was $47,500, a large sum. I have no doubt that if the government wished to part with that property to-day, they could sell it for a sum in excess of that amount. But I would much prefer, instead of^ this being sold, that an additional quantity of land adjoining the present site be purchased, and I did recommend to the late Minister of Public Works that an additional property, which I think is available there, be purchased. I must say that in hay own experience with the ex-Minister of Public Works, no request was made to the city of Saskatoon for a grant of land for drill hall purposes; and I assume that
he had in mind the fact that the case of Saskatoon was different from that of Moosejaw and Regina in the respects I have mentioned.

I would like to point out that the city of Lethbridge donated some lots to the government for the purpose of erecting an armoury, and there has been a vote for the last couple of years for that purpose, but it has been dropped this year. Now Lethbridge is anxious to have an armoury , its city council appropriated certain lots for that purpose, and there is a good deal of disappointment on account of the vote not being in the estimates this year.
I may say in connection with the recent militia conference held here, -that the view was expressed that the only way in which we can stimulate interest in the volunteer militia in western Canada is to provide these buildings, so as to bring about social surroundings for the men who go into volunteer service in the different battalions of the militia. In the city of Lethbridge they have established a battery of field artillery, but they are practically without a place for their drill and for their equipment, and have been expecting from the government an armoury by reason of the special vote -recently passed. I would urge the Minister of Public Works to consider the matter of drill halls in western Canada from this standpoint, as I _ think it will stimulate interest in the militia, and encourage the officers who are taking part in the work of the field battery and infantry corps, in their efforts to build up a good strong force there. My city is in very much the same position as pointed out by the hon. member for Moosejaw, only we have gone so far as to make a grant of land to the Dominion government, and are waiting for an armoury to be constructed. It is a very valuable property that has been granted to the government for this purpose, and I hope the Minister of Public Works will consider this matter when the supplementary estimates are being prepared.

I listened with attention to what has been said by the two last speakers and certainly will give heed to their observations. We intend to satisfy the population of the northwest as soon as possible. with regard to armouries. There is no doubt that we want our militia properly organized and that we must proceed in the way indicated. But my hon. friends must remember that a great many are called and few chosen in the matter of estimates. We try to provide in every part of' the country as far as the present resources of the Dominion admit. I must say that the demands for improvements in connection with transportation are the main

cause that this year many of these items are left out.
Humboldt public building, $25,000.

I would ask the minister's attention to the matter of a small public building provided for in the estimates of the late government and renewed in his own estimates for this year but not included in these estimates. This is for the construction of a telegraph office, postoffice and North-west Mounted Police station at a place called Gravel, 75 miles south of Moosejaw. The money was voted, the late government committed themselves to this work and the new government did so by renewing the estimates for the present year, but there is no provision for the coming year. As a matter of fact the contract has been let and signed and up to a few weeks ago there was no thought of recalling that contract. That contract will, of course, hold good in law. The vote will lapse in the spring and there is no provision for going on with the work.
If the contract is let, the government is committed and will have to provide in some way for the payment of the contractor.
Will the minister give me the information in regard to this pa,-ticular vote in the near future?
I will.

The vote for this public building at Humboldt was in the' estimates last year. During the summer the lands agent at Humboldt pointed out to me that proper provision was not made in the plans prepared by the Public Works Department for the Dominion Lands service in that new public building. Three services were to be housed by this building, the postoffice, the Dominion Lands office and the port of entry. The agent at Humboldt who, although he is a good Tory, was appointed by the late Minister of the Interior and who is a good servant as well, called my attention to this omission. I asked the Interior Department to take the matter up with the Public Works Department and have the defect in the plans remedied, but I have had no information 4s to whether or not such a change has been made. Would the minister ascertain whether the necessary representations have been made to his department?
I shall do so. This building is being erected not only for the postoffice and customs, but for a public lands office, and I think therefore provision must have been made as my hon. friend suggests.

I
Lethbridge public building, mew, $100,000.

I have no objection to offer to this public building but I would impress on the minister that we have been looking for this post office for some time, and are in absolute need of it. The floor space in the post office in the city of Lethbridge, with a population of 10,000, is about half the size of Room 16.
Lethbridge is a growing city, and the post office accommodation there is at the present time a disgrace to the country. A site has already been purchased and I would ask the minister if he will proceed with the erection of the new post office at once.
My hon. friend (Mr. Buchanan) is very fortunate in what has been provided for his constituency, there are others not so well served.
What is the total estimated cost of the Lethbridge post office?

Does the government intend to erect a new post office at Macleod this year? The post office accommodation in _ that growing city which is becoming quite a large railway centre is utterly inadequate. The late government purchased a site and I would ask what the present government intends to do?

As soon as our resources win admit of it we will provide for the want mentioned by the hon. member.
K'egina-armoury and drill hall, $50,000.
Have the plans been prepared for this building?
I think so, but I cannot say positively now.
What is the total estimated cost of this armoury?
I cannot say at the present moment, but these armouries generally cost between $50,000 and $100,000.

I know the late government had plans prepared in the department for an armoury estimated to cost $130,000, and the other day the Minister of Militia told me in the House that it was not the intention of the present government to carry out these specifications because such a building would not be sufficient to meet the needs of an important city like Regina.
That must have encouraged my hon. friend.
It did, and I am anxious now to know how much more than $130,000 is to be spent by the present government on that armoury and drill hall. I hope the minister will get me that information soon.

I shall endeavour to.
Sbrathcona public building, $30,000.
This building is now almost completed and it was the intention of the late government to put a. clock in the tower. Will the present Minister of Public Works carry out that intention?
Are these clocks not manufactured in Canada?

They are not. They 'are made only in England and in the United States, and I think the 'cheapest can be got in England.
Weyburn public building, $15,000.
The contractor for this building was at one time ordered to stop work, and I would ask the minister if he lias since given the contractor instructions to proceed.
I am under the impression that the work on that building is at present proceeding.
Will the minister ascertain and miaike sure of that?
I shall.

[DOT] The late government purchased a site for a building in the town of Camrose and an 'appropriation appeared in the former estimates to erect a building there, but that vote has been withdrawn from these estimates. What is the intention of the government with respect to the Camrose public building?
If the site has been purchased we will keep it and endeavour to utilize it.

The late government provided $25,000 in the estimates for an immigration building at Calgary, which showed that it was impressed with the necessity of a substantial building for that purpose in Calgairy. I urge upon the Minister of Public Works the desirability of providing for the erection of that building in the .supplementary estimates. I 'also wish to know if it is his intention to proceed with the public building at Athabasca.

I shall make a note and
give my hon. friend the information later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to give me some further information regarding the votes for public buildings in Vegreville and Lloydminister. Last year there were sums voted for public buildings at these points, but these items have been dropped from the estimates of this year. I put a question on the order paper asking what were the intentions of the government regarding these buildings and why they did not appear in the estimates for i912-13. The answer given to me was that the government would proceed with them as soon as circumstances would permit. Would the hon. gentleman Ibe kind enough to explain what he meant? Vegreville is a central distributing point for the mails for miles on either side. It was expected last year that this building would be erected. A site was purchased and the late Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) promised that the work would begin last year. I was, therefore, much surprised to find no provision for it in the estimates.

All I can say is that we have a great many places which require public buildings, and it is impossible to supply them all. We are only to-day beginning to provide for public buildings in seme of the older provinces where there has been necessity for them since the last 25 years. In my own constituency, a public building there has not yet been finished, and I am asking for a vote to finish it. It was unfinished in 1896 inside and outside. It has not yet been furnished with a clock, although there is a place specially prepared for one. As soon as possible I will provide for the two places mentioned. But I can only provide for a certain amount of works.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Might we hope that the minister will place an item in the supplementary estimates of this year to go on with this work?
Hope springs eternal in the human breast.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course the town of Vegreville has only a population of about 1,000, but a great deal of valuable mail matter passes through the post office there. That post office is now in the centre of a frame building, and the people and the postmaster are very much afraid lest great damage might be caused to a large amount of postal matter there through fire or other cause.
I shall make a note of my hon friend's 'suggestions.

I would like to emphasize what my hon. friend has said. He has hardly enlarged sufficiently, on the importance of this particular point. It is a railway junction. A branch of the Canadian North-

ern leads to Calgary from the main line, and it is a distributing point for the 'mail to a large territory to the north extending not less than a hundred miles through a settled country. Its importance therefore, as a mail distributing centre, is altogether out of proportion to its population.
Public buildings, British Columbia, $724,000.

I notice that British Columbia is the only province in which in 1912-13 there is a vote in excess of 1911-12. Is this a tribute to the victory of the hon. minister's friends there in September last, or is there any real necessity for these buildings?

I am surprised that my hon. friend should ask such a question. The prospective opening of the Panama canal, it is expected, will increase business immensely in Victoria and Vancouver.
katchewan and Alberta. I would not like to _ attribute the large vote this year for British Columbia to the fact that it is represented in this House by a solid phalanx of Tories, but I think the public generally in our prairie provinces may come to the conclusion that they are being penalized because they sent so few supporters of the present government to this House.

If my hon. friend's statement were carried over the past four or five years, I think he would find that things are pretty fairly equalized.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. BORDEN, moved the adjournment of the House.

If the increase of vote goes by the increase of population, my hon. friend has not looked over the records carefully, because I find that whereas the increase in population in Alberta has been a larger percentage than anywhere else in the Dominion, the appropriation for public buildings has gone down considerably, while that of British Columbia has gone up. I think we might have another explanation from my hon. friend.

The only other explanation is the law of compensation. My hon. friend knows that British Columbia has not been very generously dealt with in the past few years. This is a government of retribution and of justice.
If my hon. friend would amend that statement by striking out the word ' justice,' he would be more accurate.

I would like to emphasize the statement expressed by the hon. member for Edmonton with regard to the treatment of the prairie provinces in these estimates. In the estimates for 1912-13 the total for public buildings for the two provinces of: Saskatchewan and Alberta, which are represented in this House by 17 members, is $746,000, while the amount for British Columbia alone is $724,000, almost an equal amount to that for these two provinces. I do not think there is anything in the argument that the province of British Columbia has not been justly dealt with hitherto, because I find that in the estimates for 1911-12 the amount for British Columbia was $538,000, while the amount for Saskatchewan and Alberta together was $813,000. In other words, British Columbia was given a great deal more than half of the total for Sas-Mr. OLIVER.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of making a personal explanation on a question privilege re the case of smuggling referred to in the ' Montreal Star ' of the 12th and 19th iinstant. In its issue of the 29th instant appears the following:
Ottawa, January 29.-In the House this afternoon, the Hon. J. D. Reid, Minister of Customs, will give an affirmative answer to the following question put by Mr. G. H. Baker, of Brome
(1) Has the Minister of Customs taken cognizance of an article which appeared in the Montreal 'Star' of January 12, under the caption ' M.P.'s name is mentioned in a smuggling case'?
(2) Are the statements, as communicated to the Department of Customs, substantially as alleged in the said newspaper article?
To both queries the answer will be ' Yes.'
Mr. Speaker, I would say that I know nothing about the purchasing of those goods, nor the sending for them until the day following the seizure; and I am in no way responsible for this transaction. I was not aware of the bringing of those goods into Canada, and had ho connection with the transaction directly or indirectly.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
Wednesday, January 31, 1912.
